contract_matched_ingest.definition: Rounds 1-3 compared gigi under a 100-durability-ack contract (1,000-row batches, one WAL fsync per batch) against sqlite under a 1-ack contract (one transaction). Round 4 runs BOTH matched pairs on the same 100k dataset, same records, same order.

gigi_embedded.mechanism: single engine.batch_insert(100k records) — one WAL append pass + one fsync (+1 checkpoint-marker fsync at end of the same call, disclosed)

sqlite.mechanism: one BEGIN + executemany + COMMIT (round-1 cell, re-timed)

duckdb.mechanism: INSERT INTO txns SELECT FROM read_csv(...) — round-1 shape, CSV parse inside the clock (disclosed)

gigi_embedded.mechanism: engine.batch_insert in 1,000-row batches — 100 calls, one WAL fsync per call (the round-3b embedded cell of record, re-timed)

sqlite.mechanism: BEGIN + executemany(1000) + COMMIT per chunk — 100 transactions, journal defaults

duckdb.mechanism: BEGIN + executemany(1000) + COMMIT per chunk — 100 transactions, row-wise prepared statements

store_lane_disclosures: CONTRACT MATCHING (round-4 clause 1): rounds 1-3 timed gigi under a 100-durability-ack contract against sqlite under a 1-ack contract. This file carries both matched pairs for the stores; the two gigi lanes come from the vs_stores_embedded binary (--batch-rows 100000 for one-ack; default 1000 for many-ack) and are reported side by side with these, never mixed across contracts.

MANY-ACK 'ack' definitions per system, honestly different in kind: sqlite COMMIT under journal_mode=delete + synchronous=full (fsync-backed rollback-journal commit per chunk); duckdb COMMIT of its WAL per chunk (durability semantics per duckdb defaults, version recorded); gigi batch_insert = WAL append + one fsync per call. Each system pays its own real per-ack cost; none is normalized to another's.

duckdb MANY-ACK uses row-wise prepared-statement executemany per chunk — NOT duckdb's idiomatic columnar bulk path. That is the honest shape of a 100-transaction contract from pre-parsed Python rows; the ONE-ACK lane shows duckdb's idiomatic path (read_csv, CSV parse inside the clock, as in round 1).

sqlite lanes reuse run_sqlite.py's DDL/INSERT/fresh_connection verbatim (txn_id PRIMARY KEY maintained during ingest, fresh file DB per rep, %TEMP% local disk outside the OneDrive-synced tree); duckdb lanes reuse run_duckdb.py's likewise.
All lanes in-process, strictly serial, GC handled uniformly by eval_common.warmup_plus_reps; this runner aborts if anything answers on 127.0.0.1:3143.

post_fix_ingest_profile.method: scratch instrumented build: nanosecond accumulators around the four phases of Engine::batch_insert (schema coercion; WAL append loop = serialize + CRC + buffered write; Wal::sync = BufWriter flush + fsync, all call sites incl. checkpoint markers; in-memory store.batch_insert with the field_index/bp_reverse maintenance sub-timed). 1 untimed warmup + 3 timed reps; split aggregated over the 3 timed reps. Sources restored byte-identical after the build (verified); never committed.
disclosures: Instrumented binary ingests at 185,511 rows/s median vs 197,525 pristine (same session) — ~6% observer overhead, mostly the two per-record Instant reads around the index-maintenance window; the split is read against the instrumented total.
fsync bucket = every Wal::sync call inside the timed window: 100 per-batch data syncs + 10 checkpoint-marker syncs (checkpoint_interval=10,000).
index_maintenance is a sub-bucket of the in-memory store phase (bp_reverse + field_index upkeep for the txn_id secondary index).

honest_summary.one_ack_lane: Contract-matched gigi LOSES the one-ack lane to sqlite: 431,697 vs 515,531 rows/s median (1.19x behind; both a single durability ack on the same pre-parsed 100k rows). With fsync amortized to ~zero in this lane, the remaining gap is gigi's per-record CPU work — the profile names it: in-memory store insert 19.8% + txn_id secondary-index maintenance 12.9% + WAL serialize/CRC/buffered-write 12.2% of batch_insert time (measured under the many-ack profile; the same CPU phases run per record in both lanes). gigi one-ack beats duckdb one-ack (276,543, CSV parse in-clock as disclosed since round 1).
honest_summary.many_ack_lane: Contract-matched gigi WINS the many-ack lane: 197,525 vs sqlite 83,785 (2.36x) vs duckdb 4,187 rows/s (100 fsync-backed commits each; per-system ack semantics disclosed — sqlite journal_mode=delete/synchronous=full, duckdb WAL commit, gigi WAL append + fsync per call).
honest_summary.asymmetry_resolved: Rounds 1-3 compared gigi's 100-ack cell against sqlite's 1-ack cell. Matched both ways: sqlite's round-1 headline (previously ~5.3x, then 3.3x over gigi) becomes 1.19x at equal 1-ack contracts, and inverts to 0.42x (gigi 2.36x ahead) at equal 100-ack contracts.
honest_summary.one_ack_payload_note: No payload/serialization limit was hit: a single engine.batch_insert call with all 100k records succeeded (finding clause satisfied — nothing to work around). Disclosed: the one-ack call performs 1 data fsync + 1 checkpoint-marker fsync at end of call (checkpoint_interval=10,000).
honest_summary.bin_sweep: STABLE per the locked claim (max |delta| within {8,12,16} = 0.0185 <= 0.05). Context values: PR-AUC decreases monotonically with bin count (6: 0.6735 ... 24: 0.6271); 12 is not a cherry-picked peak — 6 and 8 both score higher. The 12-bin run reproduced the round-3b committed cell PR-AUC 0.6531 exactly.
